input_text: I don't remember hearing about Vellum anywhere before Steam pushed it to my recommendations, citing Roboquest as a similar title. It's a highly-competently-designed third-person roguelite shooter with a surprising amount of quality of life features and little cosmetic flourishes, some you might not even find in other quality examples of roguelite shooters. It's got up to four player coop, which you won't find in Roboquest (limited to 2 player) or Ziggurat 2, Immortal Redneck or Battle Shapers (No coop whatsoever). It's got the ability to reconnect to a multiplayer run in progress if you get dropped, which I haven't seen in ANY coop roguelites. Vellum casts the players as wizards of pen and ink, the Scribes of an endless magical library, whose tomes are gateways to worlds of fiction brought to life, but are threatened by dark creatures known as the Torn. The tomes kept in this libary act as the various rogue runs, each with unique gameplay mutators. A choice of ink color acts as your character class, providing passive abilities and modifiers to your choice of primary and secondary spells- one generates mana, and the other consumes it. Combat is of the type of rogue that I prefer, where it is balanced around your character frequently taking damage and offering various means to mitigate this- regenerating shields, stacks of damage resistance called "Varnish", the red ink class's lifesteal mechanic, etc. The library itself acts as a playable hub area in the vein of the Space Rig in Deep Rock Galactic or the Basecamp in Roboquest. Here you can find stations to change your equipped ink color or spells, and upgrade your "ink level", unlocking new passive buffs and perks, called "inscriptions." Customizing the appearance of your Scribe is also possible, with different helmets, robes, spellbooks and back accessories. Completing new tomes for the first time unlocks various features and interactables around the library, such as target dummies to gauge your damage output. There's even a nook set aside for each player to customize with decorations like furniture, paintings and the like. The commitment to the literary theme runs deep, with most mechanics, enemies and other elements having some kind of literary term to denote them- Enemy groups include Splices, Tangents and Ravings, the requisite roguelike perks are called "Pages", The yellow ink class has a critical hit mechanic referred to as "Flourish", the blue ink class has damage-over-time effects referred to as "Blot", you can get a bonus for using a specific spell and/or playing a specific tome called "Suggested Reading," and so on. These terms are almost always explained adequately and an in-game help text is available for, *ahem*, further reading. Additional mutators, called "Bindings", can be selected before a run, offering increased combat difficulty but commeasurately increased rewards of Quillmarks and Guild coins. The former is used for purchasing new spells, inks and upgrades, while the latter is for cosmetic purchases such as helmets, robes and furnishings for your nook. There are of course, no microtransactions, but who would put those in a roguelite? Uniquely, Vellum also offers endgame raid dungeons in the various Torn realms, which as of this writing I have only scratched the surface of. Much like an actual MMO raid, they appear to require a degree of team coordination much higher then the more casual tome runs. Vellum is stylish and fun to play and I highly recommend it to any fans of shooters or action roguelites.

input_text: This is a nice, casual game. The game methodology is fairly straightforward. They mix up hexagonal, colored wheels, and then you put them back in order. The hexes are in color (there is a colorblind option as well that includes patterns on the hexes) and the hub of each of the wheels tells you what hex colors go there. There are also mixed colors (yellow and red = orange; blue and yellow = green; red and blue = purple). The mixed colored hexes are, as you’ve probably figured out, for where the wheels overlap. The first two puzzle rounds show you how you will solve the remainder of the puzzles, and then you go through four grades of 12 puzzles. PRO: Very easy to learn, very relaxing and enjoyable. Good graphic representation. CON: No additional downloadable puzzles. Once you’ve gone through the 48 puzzles you can go into the options menu reset so that you can run through them again, but there is not a more difficult level to put to the puzzles. I would have loved to see more combinations. Worth the money? I would say a bit high, but I would like the programmers to give me more content so I would say it is fair enough. Would I pick it up on a Steam sale? In a heartbeat!!

input_text: Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart was a new but very exciting experience for me! It was not just my first Ratchet & Clank game but also my first third-person shooter, and because of that, I did not expect to enjoy this game anywhere as much as I did! This expectation was due to the fact that I am really not good at combat in video games as a whole and I thought this would prevent me from enjoying this game, however, R&C:RA’s great difficulty options, as well as the game not being condescending about said lower difficulties, allowed me to enjoy the game at one of the lower difficulties. I personally found every aspect of this game to just be plain fun! From the gameplay, including the game mechanics, to all the collectables (my favourite video game genre is collect-a-thon platformers after all!), to the animation (so pretty and detailed!), to the writing (I laughed out loud multiple times while playing) to even the character designs (was partial to the robots as I really enjoy robots in animated media, but I think all the character designs are interesting). If like me, you have never played a Ratchet & Clank game (or a third-person shooter for that matter) then in my personal opinion I think this game is a very good place to start. Highly recommend. 10/10

input_text: It's more of Paladins VR than Overwatch VR: laggy mess with barely functional matchmaking but incredibly fun to play. Larcenauts succeeds at being a hero shooter: every class is unique and feels overpowered in its own way. Current roster has 9 heroes including archer and melee brawler. The balance is not perfect, but it's a work in progress. The gameplay is fast paced constant action: grappling points and class abilities provide fast movement while objectives discourage sitting in one place for too long. However infrequent server side lags can destroy all the fun: they range from small delays and desync to huge lag spikes that render a game unplayable for up to a minute. Shooting feels arcadey but enjoyable and there a lot of accessibility settings. I especially appreciate optional button press reloading, since Reverb G2 controllers are horrible for manual reloading. Player base is not too big for a cross-platfrom game: full 6v6 matches are only possible during peak hours. The rest of the time it will be about 3-8 players in a session with empty slots filled with bots. And AI is terrible: they can barely walk without getting stuck all the time. With small play base come issues with matchmaking: in every match experienced players will be mixed with newbies making new player experience particularly painful at times. And to add insult to injury Larcenauts matchmaking can't even distribute human players between teams equally. There are a lot of 2v4, 3v5, etc and the system doesn't bother to change team distribution between matches most of the time.

input_text: I umm'd and ahh'd as to whether to review this as recommended or not for a couple of weeks after completing. I ultimately erred on the side of recommending, as the game does deserve more attention than I feel it's gotten, but the recommendation is almost conditional on doing the YOLO (which has it's own drawbacks beyond just being another stupid platformer YOLO). Further detail below. For a casual player, the experience is short-lived. You get to the end, you get your food of choice, and you're done. This takes under 2 hours for a first play through. The additional modes do little to liven the game up, adding a new gimmick that changes how the game is played in some way that ultimately just gives the same experience with a slightly different shade of paint over the top. If your goal is to 'just get to the end', I'd recommend against the game. Where the game shines though is in figuring out cycles, figuring out approaches to make consistent that which seems like some haphazard BS the first play time through. This outcome is only achieved through the YOLO (endurance mode), assuming you don't trivialise the exercise through the use of accessibility options. I love that accessibility options are there enabling everyone to play how they feel best suits their needs, but for me, they took away from the one element of the game that made it worthwhile. I ultimately came back to the game to beat it without just the intent of ticking off 'another steam hundo'. When viewed with the lens of "I need to not die" (rather than just getting to the end), the sections are varied, the hazards are interesting, and the platforming is... well... inconsistent. Unfortunately whilst the 'levels' are interesting, the game decides it doesn't want to behave consistently. Some plays through a full jump won't clear 2x blocks, sometimes you'll get stuck in a corner, and other times you'll get pushed back by an invisible wall (that for some reason never happened in the 10hrs you'd played previously?). I've not been so frustrated with a game before due to the game itself, rather than something attributed to my own skills. So with all these caveats.... The game is flawed, the non-YOLO challenge is limited, the price is high for the content and design compared to other games in the genre... but it's a good game. A bit unpolished, a bit janky, a bit unfulfilling as a casual player.. but at the heart of it, it's a good game.

input_text: Entomophobia Entomophobia is a bug-slaying bullet-heaven where you collect a variety of unique weapons and upgrades unlike anything I have seen in a bullet-heaven so far. It currently has a few issues but it is early-access so they may be addressed by full release, it is also fairly easy once you know what upgrades to take and I found myself afking to farm the 1,000,000 kills achievement. Gameplay There are 8 characters in this game each with different stats, starting weapons and abilities, you also get a choice of gun to take with you, of which there are 5. Characters and guns can be unlocked by either completing achievements or buying them with meta-currency. There are a tonne of weapons in this game and they all act and are visually unique to anything I have seen in other bullet-heavens, how many games can you slay enemies with cornflakes, waffles and lemons while using a sniper rifle? You can take up to 5 weapons and passives total, as well as a stackable augment at every level. There's currently no way to tell when a weapon is max and there are no rerolls or banishes to help you get what you want. There are 3 maps in the game that all play basically the same as one another, the only real difference being slightly less space to move around, which is only more difficult for the first few minutes of each run. Enemies come in the same waves at the same time in each run, with each run lasting 20 minutes. Most enemies play the same but a few will back away from you while shooting projectiles and bosses come every 4 minutes or so dropping you extra upgrades. You get Shells while you play which can be spent on new characters, weapons and meta-upgrades, there are only 5 meta-upgrades that are very passive, by the time I had killed 1,000,000 bugs for the achievement I had an extra 22,000 shells that I couldn't spend on everything. There needs to be another sink to spend these on, preferably more combat upgrades. The game in it's current state is too easy, it becomes trivial after about 5 minutes if you know what upgrades to pick, I would personally like some sort of difficulty modifiers similar to 20 Minutes Till Dawn's Darkness levels that allow for a bit more of a challenge. Achievements (18/18) 95% of your time with the achievements in this game will be spent farming the 1 million bug kills, it helps to play on the River map as enemies are pushed from outside the map quite close to you and you can average around 25,000 kills per run, It took me a total of 30 hours to grind both kills and deaths. Music/sound There are a few different songs in the game that fit well, but they get repetitive after a while. Settings/Accessibility/Misc No rebindable controls. Auto-aim available. In-game achievement menu to see progress. Enemy outlines, projectile enemies are visually distinct. Settings to change the overlay colour of character, enemies, background and dangerous objects (but you can't scroll down far enough to change the dangerous objects one), these could be useful for people with colour-blindness. TL;DR Bug-slaying bullet-heaven where you collect a variety of unique weapons and upgrades. Needs more difficulty options. 3 maps that play very samey, 8 characters, 5 guns, tonnes of weapons. No rerolls/banishes. A few meta-upgrades. Very grindy achievements. Check out my Curator page

input_text: Strange Horticulture is an exquisitely crafted puzzle and exploration game that invites players into a world where botany meets mystery and folklore. Developed with an evident passion for plants and storytelling, the game offers a deeply atmospheric experience centered around running a curious herb shop in a remote and eerie village. From the moment you step into the shoes of the shopkeeper, Strange Horticulture weaves together the delicate art of plant identification with a compelling narrative that unfolds through cryptic requests, ancient secrets, and supernatural undertones. For players who enjoy slow-burning mysteries, detailed research mechanics, and atmospheric world-building, this game offers a unique and memorable adventure. At its heart, Strange Horticulture tasks players with running an old plant shop where villagers come seeking rare and sometimes bizarre herbs for their ailments or needs. The gameplay revolves around careful observation and deduction: you must examine the physical descriptions and symptoms provided by customers, then match these clues to an ever-growing compendium of plants. This process is intellectually engaging, requiring players to study botanical illustrations, cross-reference characteristics, and make informed decisions under subtle time pressure. Unlike many traditional puzzle games, Strange Horticulture rewards patience and curiosity, allowing you to gradually build knowledge rather than rush through challenges. One of the standout features of the game is its beautifully detailed plant database, which functions as both a tool and a narrative device. Each plant entry is meticulously designed, featuring hand-drawn artwork, botanical descriptions, historical uses, and notes on folklore and mythology. This encyclopedic approach immerses players in a rich world where plants carry meaning beyond their physical properties—some hold mystical powers, others are tied to local legends, and many possess symbolic weight in the unfolding story. The research element feels authentic and satisfying, giving the player a genuine sense of discovery akin to being a scholar or apothecary. The narrative in Strange Horticulture is subtle and layered, revealed gradually through the interactions with villagers, hidden notes, and the enigmatic mysteries surrounding the shop and its surroundings. The game cleverly intertwines folklore and horror, creating an unsettling atmosphere that lingers beneath the surface of its pastoral setting. Each customer’s request and story peel back another layer of the village’s secrets, encouraging players to pay close attention to dialogue and environmental cues. The story doesn’t rely on bombastic twists but rather builds tension through implication and the eerie connections between people and plants, making for an immersive and thought-provoking experience. Visually, the game is a triumph of minimalist design paired with intricate detail. The art style employs muted, earthy tones and finely drawn illustrations that evoke old botanical manuscripts and Victorian-era herbals. This aesthetic choice not only suits the game’s thematic focus but also enhances the mood of quiet mystery and antiquarian charm. The shop interface is clean and intuitive, allowing easy access to plant specimens, notes, and customer requests without overwhelming the player. Subtle animations and environmental details, such as rustling leaves or flickering candlelight, contribute to the ambiance without distracting from the core gameplay. Sound design plays a crucial role in building Strange Horticulture’s immersive atmosphere. The soundtrack consists of gentle, ambient melodies interspersed with natural sounds like wind, birdsong, and distant footsteps, all combining to create a serene yet slightly unsettling backdrop. Audio cues guide players through interactions and heighten moments of revelation or tension. The voice acting, while sparing, is well-executed, lending authenticity to the villagers’ varied personalities and enhancing the narrative depth. While Strange Horticulture excels in atmosphere and intellectual challenge, it may not appeal to all players due to its deliberately slow pace and cerebral focus. The absence of traditional action or urgent gameplay means the experience is more meditative than adrenaline-fueled. Some players might find the reliance on textual clues and botanical details a bit daunting or niche, requiring careful reading and note-taking to progress effectively. Additionally, the game’s open-ended puzzle design can sometimes lead to trial and error, especially for those unfamiliar with botanical terminology, which might disrupt the otherwise smooth flow. Technically, the game is well-optimized and runs smoothly across a variety of hardware. The interface is responsive, and the game’s minimalistic design ensures quick loading times and stable performance. The developers have also included accessibility options such as adjustable text sizes and colorblind modes, demonstrating thoughtful attention to player needs and comfort. In conclusion, Strange Horticulture is a beautifully realized and intellectually stimulating puzzle game that offers a rare blend of botanical scholarship, atmospheric storytelling, and quiet mystery. Its carefully crafted mechanics, evocative art, and immersive sound design combine to create a game that feels both scholarly and hauntingly poetic. While its slow pace and niche subject matter might limit its appeal to more casual or action-oriented players, those who appreciate thoughtful exploration and narrative depth will find Strange Horticulture to be a richly rewarding and unforgettable experience. It stands as a testament to how games can educate and intrigue simultaneously, cultivating a deep appreciation for the natural world and the mysteries hidden within it. Rating: 9/10

input_text: When I first saw COATED in the Upcoming section, it looked interesting enough to bookmark for further examination upon release. I'm grown hesitant to actually buy day-of-release games, expecially if no discount is offered. But when I saw the following message on the Store Page, the decision was made: "If you got a good experience, don't forget to mention that "Only" if you've a free moment. But in case you got a bad experience, then you "MUST" speak about it, that way you'll get better games next time." This degree of commitment made the purchase decision easy. And the first few minutes of play indicates that this may just turn out to be a very pleasant game, at a fair price (even without discount.) One thing I've learned is that the most important aspect of any new game is a concerned DEV. I wonder, however, if I'll be the only player to accidentally loose all my save data by simply attempting to exit the OPTIONS screen. I'm not sure that gameplay should be a component of the setup menus. For small children, or their beginner parents wanting to bond, this sort of rage-inducing feature might be a bad idea. If Blind Color is the same as Color Blind, having 2 levels to select for accessibility is a wonderfully kind, as well as marketable, feature. Though COATED is advertised as playable by children, don't be misled. This game is challenging enough to be interesting to gamers of any age or skill level. (I hope to update this review soon.) Thank you.

input_text: Fun mix of typing with horror, though it desperately needs a brightness slider. Try the demo to check if you can actually see anything first. I got this on offer through the Bloody Keys bundle, since I already had Blood Typers . I like typing, and typing games, but usually have a very low tolerance for genuinely scary horror. I can handle campy over the top stuff like Blood Typers and the Resident Evil games, but have never been able to get far in games like Amnesia and Phasmophobia . I have gotten all the way through to the first possible ending in Dead Letter Dept , so I think it's safe to say that it's on the lower end of scariness, though there are some slight jump-scares with static and visual effects on the screen. So far none of them have come with a loud noise though, which is usually the bigger problem. I did resort to walking backwards or while facing the floor near the end of the game though, so there might be things I deliberately missed. It's very fun and effective as a typing game, with an accessibility option to turn off cursive writing and an auto-suggest program to make sure you've typed a real address. Expect to have a lower WPM than you would normally manage though. Even if you're fearless, you're probably going to want to stop to read and process some of the things you're typing up. My main complaint is that it needs a brightness slider. I had to turn my monitor's brightness up from 20 to 100 to see anything, when the 20 setting has been perfect for every other game I play and video I watch.

input_text: Reviews for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing Overall Rating: 5/10 Gameplay Rating: 4/10 Accessibility Rating: 10/10 Overall rating is a combination of the gameplay (mechanics and story) and accessibility (how the game includes deaf/hoh gamers). General Gameplay Dysfunctional Systems is a graphic novel game that tells its story and involves the gamer in a story that plays out via text and images. You are Winter Harrison, a 14-year-old girl from a utopian world who serves as an interplanar mediator. She finds herself in Sule, a world entering into conflict that she and her mentor, Cyrus, must help resolve. If you're new to graphic novel games, the pacing is slow and story-driven. As these games go, Dysfunctional Systems' episode 1 is a short, simple introduction to the story that, though somewhat involving in its events, leaves the player left short-changed on any real development of character or story. Even so, if you have the money to spare on something you know is incomplete, this game is a small treat that can, in some ways, make up for its brevity. Replayability/Sequels While this episode has a promising start to something that could be interesting, it seems unclear whether or not there will be additional episodes following this one. General Accessibility Accessibility Options Options can be accessed before the game begins, allowing you control of game settings. Music and sound volume are controlled separately and can be muted altogether. The game plays out over text boxes. Text speed, textbox opacity and color, and the ability to skip text are all available options, giving gamers control over the pace of the game. Subtitles & Captions Dysfunctional Systems is captioned completely from beginning to end and the story plays out in text, which does not advance until the gamer decides to do so. Captions include the speaker's name and quotes for directly spoken text. Narrated text is provided without quotes and a name, so I assume it's the main character (Winter) thinking or addressing the gamer directly. The game's captions are very true to spoken word, so any deaf/hoh who do not frequently use English to communicate may find it tedious at times. Chatting/Communicating Dysfunctional Systems is a single player game; no communication/chatting options available. --- Visit Games Reviews for the Deaf/HoH [URL]

input_text: Prismatica is a color theory puzzle game where colors are scrambled and you have to rotate the gears to move the colored tiles around until they are in their appropriate places. This includes their combinations as well (example: If a red and a yellow gear have shared tiles, those tiles will turn orange). There are four total sections, each with a standard and challenge category of 12 puzzles (so there are a total of 48 puzzles that are the same in both standard mode and challenge mode). Standard mode gives you your first of three stars for that level, and challenge mode asks you to finish the same puzzle under a certain number of moves and under a certain amount of time to get the other two stars. I finished the game with all puzzles at three stars in about 11 hours. I definitely enjoyed my time with this game. I think it's great that there is a standard and challenge mode. A nice feature they included is that you don't have to finish both of the challenges at once to get the other two stars. You can focus on one at a time if you would prefer, because once you complete a task it gives you the star. This is much more preferable to having to be conscious of the moves you are making, while still moving as quickly as possible. When it came to the challenges, I felt there were levels that gave you plenty of time/number of moves to complete it, but there were also some others that felt like it didn't give quite enough wiggle room for mistakes. I did find, however, that after moving forward in standard mode, the challenge mode for earlier levels became easier to handle because of the extra practice I had gotten, so I recommend continuing standard or just jumping to a different challenge level if you are having trouble. The game settings are pretty simple, but this isn't really an issue because of the minimalist nature of the game. There is a button to toggle music on and off and another button to toggle sound effects on and off. There is also a colorblind mode that puts symbols over the colors for clearer matching. I ended up muting sound effects because they became a bit irritating to listen to. I kept the music on because it had enough variation and I enjoyed its upbeat nature. The fanfare that comes with completing a level filled me with so much joy and satisfaction. It made working through the puzzles very rewarding. I definitely recommend this game to those who are looking for a short but fun experience that exercises your brain. I felt myself starting to understand the required rotations necessary to move the tiles where I wanted to (In that respect I very much see how the Rubik's Cube inspired them), and at the end of each level I felt accomplished and pleased. Some may feel that the price is a little high with the amount of hours played, so if that's the case go ahead and get it on a sale, but I personally enjoyed the whole experience enough to say it's worth the full price.

input_text: I always enjoyed it for about 30 minutes per sitting. Any duration after that got repetitive and often annoying, despite how great the presentation was. Don't pay full price. The Good +Skippable splash screens +Four difficulties +Horde mode (survive waves of enemies and bosses) +Tons of options, can rebind everything, adjust UI etc +Display options to increase or decrease pixelation +Accessibility options to include invincibility +Surprisingly colorful, for the most part +Rare cutscenes are well drawn +Good music +Sound is excellent. Love the thumping of movement and bolt weapons. +Autosaves, quicksaves, and manual saves available +Squishy enemies in all levels for power trip +The servoskull has some rare but funny dialog +You can hear when a bolter magazine is nearly empty YMMV ~EULA ~The story makes no sense unless you're familiar with Warhammer ~10-12 hours for a single playthrough ~Servoskull can be distracting, even when set to low duration ~Shotgun's kinda garbage...and it's not bound to #3 ~No map ~HP, armor, weapon powerup, ammo capacity reset after each level ~The rare areas with unexpected instant death mechanics are annoying ~Many combat areas don't provide enough room to dodge well ~Falling in most pits just teleports you to nearest platform ~The angled elevator in chapter 3 was very buggy for me ~The melee attack is needlessly complicated and rather useless ~The dash doesn't work if you're on any kind of incline ~The taunt is great for RP, but pointless otherwise. This, the melee attack, and dash (if it worked on anything other than flat terrain) should have given some kind of buff or health/armor regen if used successfully. The Bad -Gets repetitive quickly, especially the first and third chapters -Game doesn't explain quirks of some weapons -More fog than Turok on the N64. Some can be turned off, but not all -The two charging enemies do ridiculous damage -The two charging enemies are usually unavoidable. Seriously. F those Aspirants. -Bosses are repeated over and over and over and over -Many bosses have infinite annoying trash spawns -Vortex grenades should have their own hotkey -Servoskull's directions are often wrong (deadend, old objective, etc) -One boss had a wall-of-text dialog that there was no chance to read in the middle of combat Played on: Win11Pro, i7-14700K, RTX5060 Ti 16GB, 32GB DDR5-6000 @ 1920x1080 using KB&M Normal difficulty

input_text: First Try on Top Hat The Video can be found here: [URL] Before recording and writing this review, I have played the game until Level 3-3 on normal mode, which took me about 30 minutes. First off, the options menu is relatively simplistic. You have 3 seperate sliders for audio options. Apart from that you can adjust the screen size(which I would not consider resolution options). Last, but by no means least, you can rebind the controls for keyboard and controller. Going into the game, the first thing I've noticed is that the dialogue is well translated and the jokes came across fairly well. The music is also quite good, the only minor complaint I have is that the looping of the music is a bit clunky. Gameplaywise I have to say that the gunplay(if can call it that way) and the platforming feel nice. The enemy variety and enemy design is simplistic, but it does the job. The bosses so far feel relatively underwhelming(the mechanic of the first one is easy to dodge, the second one is quite tedious to fight), but it might change later on. One thing I'd like to add before coming to the conclusion is that one of the "selling ponits" of the game is "Challenging. Really". So far I have to say, the game is not that challenging. It is more the case that the game is unforgivable in terms of mistakes. Since there are no savegame slots, you will only have one savegame. Apart from your progress your current lifecount is saved as well, which can end in a mess when you are only on one life bevore hitting a checkpoint. I can imagine that it is getting frustrating when you hit harder levels(or even bossfights) with only one life left. The question I suppose is: Is the game difficult, because it's genuinely difficult, or is it because of design decisions in terms of savepoints, etc? And in the case of top hat, I say, it is "difficult" for the wrong reasons. With that out of the way we come to the tl:dr: Is the game worth it? It is not a bad game that is for sure, but as I've stated above, I went about 1/3 through the game within 30 minutes, so you can say that your average playthrough will take you somewhat around 2 hours. And apart from Achievments and a higher difficulty levels there is not much replayability available. With that said, I'd say it's a definite buy at a sale, but if you are desperate for a nice action plattformer, you might consider buying this game even on full price.

input_text: It was an ok game, but very easy while also frustrating. There is no way to skip the tutorial, and even after that the game insists on holding your hand whether you want to or not. Puzzles are extremely easy throughout. HOS are ok, generally well translated, but the ones that are not are extremely confusing. Also, the misclick penalty seems to just be about number of misclicks in a row, with no timer involved. Towards the end of the game, it becomes frustratingly hard for all the wrong reasons. There are hints, but only text ones, and no map indications, so you spend most of your time running around trying to find a person with something new to say, but in most cases, which of the HOS's has reactivated. And for my taste, there were way to many of those, especially compared to the few puzzles. The hints might tell you what to do to meet your objectives, but they tended to point to the wrong ones, while also spoiling the already too easy puzzles. Two of the last few puzzles even had built in backtracking. The story is the usual kind for this kind of game, when it is there at all, but I wasn't expecting much from it. It has an ok base, honestly, but some very bad design choices made it mainly frustrating. The short bit between they stopped telling you what to do before you just had to guess where to go was ok? I honestly can't recommend it, even on sale. Hopefully the devs learn from the experience and get better with time.

input_text: The Inner World: The Last Wind Monk is a thoughtful and endearing point-and-click adventure that builds on the quirky charm of its predecessor, deepening the narrative and expanding the strange, whimsical world of Asposia. Developed by Studio Fizbin and published by Headup Games, the game offers a blend of clever puzzles, heartfelt storytelling, and richly imaginative world-building that appeals to fans of both classic adventure titles and modern narrative-driven games. While it remains grounded in traditional point-and-click mechanics, The Last Wind Monk excels by infusing its universe with emotional depth, character growth, and a surprising layer of political and philosophical commentary. The story picks up a few years after the events of the first game, once again following Robert, the unlikely hero and flute-nose monk, who has been in hiding since the rise of a fanatical regime bent on eradicating his kind. The antagonist Emil, a populist tyrant, has spread propaganda that blames the flute-noses for Asposia’s past misfortunes. Robert must now team up with returning characters like the spirited Laura and the ever-loyal pigeon Peck to find the mythical last Wind Monk and restore peace. What begins as a whimsical journey soon reveals itself to be a surprisingly poignant tale about intolerance, identity, and the misuse of power. The themes are handled delicately, balancing humor with introspection and satire with sincerity. Visually, The Last Wind Monk is a joy to behold. The hand-drawn art style, filled with odd, soft-edged characters and surreal landscapes, creates a world that feels like a cross between a children’s storybook and a surrealist painting. The environments are packed with detail and personality, from gloomy prison cells to vast underground temples and lively cityscapes. Each area feels distinct and alive, with cleverly designed layouts that encourage exploration and interaction. The animations are smooth and expressive, lending additional character to every NPC and making even minor interactions feel rewarding. The gameplay sticks closely to the genre’s roots, emphasizing item collection, environmental interaction, and puzzle-solving. What sets it apart, however, is the variety introduced through character switching. Players can control Robert, Laura, and Peck at different points, each with their own abilities and perspectives. Peck, for example, can fly into otherwise inaccessible areas, while Laura’s no-nonsense attitude often drives narrative momentum. The puzzles themselves range from simple to delightfully convoluted, often requiring players to combine items in unconventional ways or interpret dialogue clues carefully. At times, puzzle logic may feel obtuse, but the integrated hint system ensures that players who get stuck can move forward without too much frustration. The voice acting and writing deserve particular praise. The English voice cast delivers consistently strong performances, with Robert’s earnestness, Laura’s sarcasm, and Peck’s chirps and squawks all contributing to a warm and often hilarious tone. The dialogue is witty and smart, balancing slapstick humor with deeper philosophical questions. Studio Fizbin has a gift for writing dialogue that’s playful yet meaningful, often masking social commentary beneath layers of absurdity. The localization is excellent, retaining the humor and nuance of the original German version without losing cultural relevance or tone. The Inner World: The Last Wind Monk is not without flaws. Some players might find the pacing a bit slow in certain sections, especially when backtracking through areas or solving particularly complex puzzles. Additionally, while the game expands on the lore of Asposia, it relies heavily on familiarity with the first game—new players might feel slightly lost without having experienced Robert’s original journey. That said, for returning fans or those willing to dive into the world of Asposia from the start, the payoff is rich and rewarding. In conclusion, The Inner World: The Last Wind Monk is a charming and surprisingly poignant adventure that combines the classic appeal of point-and-click gameplay with modern storytelling finesse. Its unique visual style, engaging puzzles, and heartfelt narrative create an experience that’s both whimsical and reflective. It’s a game that dares to be silly while also addressing serious themes, offering a thoughtful commentary on prejudice, fear, and hope in a world that feels just fantastical enough to mirror our own. For players who appreciate narrative-driven adventures with personality, warmth, and just a touch of melancholy, this game is an easy recommendation. Rating: 8/10

There is of course replay value as well, there being two routes you can experience (or a mix thereof). Learning that this is a stand-alone entry in a game series I expect I'll be trying more titles from this developer in future.

input_text: I love Stronghold Crusader, having played a TON of it in childhood and adulthood. As games go, it's meant a lot to me over the years. Multiplayer seems to work fine, though there are latency issues that are unacceptable for a modern RTS of this price. input_text: TL;DR: Unique multiplayer, but rough around the edges. Cheaters are everywhere, the anti-cheat is as real as winning a war against a weak neighbor country in one month, and both MMR and netcode feel like they were coded by interns on their first day. Matches are long, unbalanced, and full of quitters, which is more of a design flaw than a player issue. Single player is not worth touching. Updates arrive slowly, marketed as “meaningful,” but usually fix little while breaking something else. Buy it on sale, know exactly what hole you are jumping into, and you might have some fun. Just do not expect anything close to polished or professional. Buy it for the multiplayer only, and train yourself to turn off half your brain, since rush B is always the meta. There is no real anti-cheat, so cheaters are as common as mosquitoes in summer. It got so bad that the developers had to lock the cheater report thread on Discord because they could not keep up and it was making the game, and some regions of the world, look even worse. MMR is broken, the netcode is unreliable, and it shows. Matches can last 45 minutes or more, there is no option to forfeit, and players quit constantly. The developers keep saying they will punish quitters, but the problem is not the players, it is the design. Matchmaking is sloppy, balance is inconsistent, and the so called rock paper scissors mechanic rarely applies in practice. People are not leaving because they are bad, they are leaving because nobody wants to waste nearly an hour, including the lobby and matchmaking wait, on a match that is doomed from the start. I have played over 100 matches without quitting, the only times I disconnected were due to crashes or connection issues, which is just another headache. That being said, there is nothing else quite like it. WARNO might come close in gameplay, but its community is probably just as questionable. Single player is the comedy act nobody asked for. You cannot save mid mission, some missions take hours, and the AI is both dumb and omniscient at the same time. It feels like fighting a wallhack bot that still makes terrible decisions. Funny to watch, awful to play, and definitely not worth the effort. The game goes on sale often. I pre ordered the Vanguard Edition, refunded it on launch day, and bought the Standard Edition for 20 percent less the same day. No regrets there. When it works, which is maybe 50 to 60 percent of the time, it is genuinely fun. The rest of the time you are just spinning the wheel of crashes, ragequits, and hackers. Do I recommend it? input_text: The game, when first released, was an experiment for Boomzap as they wished to branch out into the Strategy genre after having made their name with Hidden Object games. This game quickly became one of my favorite indie games and is quick and easy to pick up and play, while offering quite the challenge as you move through the campaign. They also released a mobile version of the game, and buying one version (mobile or PC) gave you the other version for free, allowing you to continue through your campaign through either method. Within the past year or so, issues arose with the authentication server, which made the game impossible to play beyond a demo like mode if you installed it on a new device. The devs indicated that it would be costly, if not impossible, to fix those issues due to the backend coding that allowed them to connect mobile and PC versions. Gratefully, though, they have worked to get the PC version back up and running, though Multiplayer needed to be disabled in order to do so. I still recommend this game as it's a fun game to play. I am by no means an expert in the Strategy genre. I have played games like Civilization, Total War, Risk, Stronghold, et al. but haven't played any with the card mechanic like this that I recall, so can't make comparisons. All I can say is that I have enjoyed this game from the start, and look forward to continuing through the campaigns at my leisure, and playing those skirmishes, which I have done a lot of. The loss of multiplayer and mobile suck, but at the end of the day, despite losing money on this experiment, the devs put forth the effort to get the PC version back up and working and are to be commended for doing so.

input_text: I stopped playing about a month ago because constant leavers killed the fun for me and my friends. Today I decided to give it another shot to see if things had improved. Spoiler: they haven’t. The following is a good example of the current state and average experience with this game: I qued up for two games. First queue: two players on the enemy team disconnected during loading and never came back. We spent 45 minutes in unfun seal-clubbing because there’s still no surrender option. Second queue: waited ~7 minutes, got kicked from the queue with a connection error. Restarted the game and queued again. Then had to wait another 7 minutes. - My own account that I previously queued with then somehow ended up on the enemy team, so I basically played against myself. - My deck that picked didn’t transfer into the match (probably because I was in the lobby twice). - Enemy players were displayed as “friendly” in chat. - I couldn’t spawn units at all! - After leaving the game, I couldn’t even rejoin. - When the match ended, I still got slapped with a full -25 ELO penalty. - Potentially had to wait another 5-7 min to find the next match - i quit instead. The gameplay itself is fun when the core game functions actually work, but that’s the problem, they rarely do. Add in constant bugs (invisible units, rubber-banding, hits not registering, LOS not working), broken reporting/anticheat, and poor connection stability… and it’s pretty clear why hardly anyone is still playing this game. I can’t really comment on the single-player aspect since I only played two missions, but it still has no save function since launch. In this state this RTS is definitely not worth a hefty 50 EUR. input_text: Diablo 4 Beta Review Rating: 8/10 After spending several hours playing the Diablo 4 beta, I can share my thoughts on what Blizzard is preparing for the full release. Overall, the beta gave a good preview of what the game will offer, with plenty of positive aspects but also a few issues that need attention before the final launch. Positives: Environment and Graphics: There’s no denying that the world of Sanctuary looks stunning. The dark and detailed atmosphere truly immerses you in the game. The lighting, the intricate cityscapes, and the dungeons, along with how the environment interacts with weather effects, are all impressive. It’s a living, breathing world that adds another layer of immersion. Combat and Gameplay: The combat system is dynamic and very satisfying. The fluidity of animations and quick response of controls make battles visceral and engaging. I played as both the Barbarian and the Sorcerer, and both classes are a lot of fun, with distinct abilities and build possibilities that encourage experimentation. The feeling of power when wiping out hordes of enemies is something the franchise has always nailed, and it’s no different here. Progression and Customization: Character progression is one of the standout features. The skill system offers deep customization, allowing players to create unique builds. The fact that every skill has a meaningful impact on gameplay ensures that players feel a constant sense of evolution, with rewards at each new level. Open World and Multiplayer: The option to play in a shared, open world with other players is one of the most interesting innovations in Diablo 4. Dynamic events, like monster invasions and boss fights, make exploration more engaging. And of course, interacting with other players, even in a non-forced way, adds an extra layer of fun. Negatives: Server Issues (Beta): As expected, the beta wasn’t free from server issues. There were times when wait times to enter the game were long, and lag hindered the experience. While these issues are common in beta phases, they still impacted the flow of gameplay and caused some frustration. Content Repetition: Although the story hooked me, I felt that some quests and side activities started to feel repetitive after a few hours. The main story quests are interesting, but the side missions often don’t offer much variety in objectives, which can become tiring for more dedicated players. Limited Beta Content: The beta, while giving a solid idea of what to expect, also left a sense of incompleteness. Some features and areas of the game were locked, meaning we couldn't experience the game in its entirety. It left me with the feeling that the core of the game will only truly shine once the full version is released. Monetization and Microtransactions (Concerns): While the beta didn’t directly showcase this, the question of microtransactions and monetization still looms large. It wasn’t clear how Blizzard will balance this aspect, especially in a game that has the potential to be a massive hit among RPG and ARPG fans. I just hope the experience isn’t negatively impacted by excessive monetization practices. Conclusion: The Diablo 4 beta at the time in 2023 left me excited for the full release. Blizzard has nailed several aspects, like combat, character progression, and creating a dynamic open world. However, some server issues and content repetition still need to be addressed. In summary, Diablo 4 has the potential to be one of the franchise’s best titles, but a few tweaks are needed to perfect it. For long-time fans of the series, it’s definitely worth keeping an eye on the official release, and I hope Blizzard can deliver a polished, varied experience.

input_text: It’s a cute game, but I fully admit that I don’t have any strong feelings about it one way or the other. Again, it’s sweet, but nothing to write home about, and I don’t know if I will be replaying any time soon. Quality wise, the art is nice, and the music can be a bit overbearing at times, but it did match the theme well enough. There were a few snippets of text here and there that confused me a bit, some were small spelling errors and there were a few that I’m not quite sure if they were typos or just figures of speech that I had never heard before, but it was nothing major and I wouldn’t say that they detracted from my overall enjoyment of the game. Really my biggest issue with the game was the progression of the story, which went WAAYY to fast for my liking. These two dudes have just met this girl and suddenly it’s all “Hey let’s date!” I mean, it even sorta gets acknowledged in game how quickly things are progressing. But again, for a $5 otome game, I wasn’t expecting an Idea Factory narrative. In conclusion: It’s a short game you can finish in less than a day, it has it’s cute moments, and the art is pretty, so go ahead and buy it if you like the beach and shirtless mermen. It's only $5 after all. On a side note: there was a scene near the beginning of the game that was unintentionally funny? It was a pan up of Crylis (The merman’s) sprite, and for some reason this merman sprite descending from the heavens was just the funniest thing to me. Don’t ask me why; it was late, I was kinda tired, and I have a terrible sense of humor.

input_text: Multi-path stories sim Using various types of stat values in each story, the player can manipulate how the story goes. Ruin the character’s life or make it as best as it can be. Praises • Emma’s story path gives some insight into the type of bullsh*t women put up with in a male-dominated workplace. • Paul’s story path demonstrates how ridiculously corrupt and hypocritical politicians are. • There is a decent amount of diversity among all the characters of the game. • The game made me chuckle a couple of times. Complaints • Lots of typos. A few sections of text left untranslated from French. Some awkward translations to English. • Imbalanced elements in gameplay. • Jenny’s story path is boring. I had so little motivation to finish it because there was nothing interesting about it. It seems like it was supposed to be about bullying and dealing with college, except bullying is rare in college; that’s more of a k-12 thing. Regardless, the point of it was just so poorly-written and weak. • (Possible Bug) During Jenny’s story path, it is not even remotely obvious how you’re supposed to inform Hamim about Mika’s internship. There are no options for it anywhere, then the two friends get upset because the event never occurs. • (Bug) During Jenny’s path, it seems like there isn’t a way to stop Mika from committing the prank, even though on the branch map, it insinuates there is. • (Bug) On Jenny’s path, the revision notes do not refresh for a new playthrough, making it impossible to know how many the player actually has for that playthrough. They do not stack through playthroughs. • While Paul’s story path addresses the importance of environmentalism, it does the typical mistake of putting the responsibility mostly on general individuals rather than the billionaires whose industries are almost entirely responsible for climate change. Furthermore, the socialist politician character in his story would’ve made that point by arguing that eliminating capitalism would absolutely lead to better environmentalism and she unrealistically makes no such argument. (I am not suggesting people should stop individually doing things that help the environment. I am just pointing out that if you want to stop the planet from burning up in a few generations, the only way to do that is to stop the billionaires and their industries. There is no other way, because it is literally them killing the planet with their industries.) • (Bug) Jordan’s story path seems entirely messed up because in order for him to confess that he’s gay to people, he needs enough morale, but he never has enough for what is required and there is seemingly no way to increase the max amount of morale. It’s just 3. I can’t tell if the bug is that there are suppose to be more or that the method of increasing the max morale is not presenting itself. But yeah, it’s impossible to confess to anyone. Considering the game was released in 2021 and there are several improvements that need to be made, I can’t recommend the game. It’s a cool concept, but executed poorly. It is seemingly impossible to get a lot of the achievements.

So far, I've only noticed this when recalling the foragers I've sent out. All somewhat small bugs, honestly. The game works fine, looks fine, and plays fine in spite of all I've mentioned; it might just need an update for polishing up and it'll be golden. input_text: This would be a decent short point and click adventure title were it not so… slapdash. The English translation is pretty engrish, though the voice acting isn't that bad. Some locations have two music tracks accidentally playing on top of another and the game characters have entirely different design and looks during in-game and cutscenes. (The protagonist alternates between having a black three-day stubble and a shaved face with silver moustache – and gains about 20 years of age!) Puzzles can be roughly divided into two categories – there's item-using puzzles that fit the world, and random bouts of sudoku and tic-tac-toe that seem there just for filler. And I had the tic-tac-toe glitch on me. It's just so half-hearted and I'm willing to give historical adventure titles quite a bit of leeway. I suppose the best thing about this game is that the journal in the inventory works as a walkthrough if you get stuck. (Oh yeah, I left the game on for an entire day by accident so that's why the long duration. It's not that long.)

input_text: This game is pretty good. There are a few issues that can be sorted out with some extra time, but for the most part it's enjoyable and solid. Will list pros and cons below. I will say, many people say the game is too easy, but I feel that they must have only played the first initial playthrough based on time spent and my own experience of how the difficulty definitely gets up there. Can recommend for anyone who enjoys a card drafting game, roguelike gameplay, and the like. PROS ~Polished and unique art style ~Very nice soundtrack ~Cards seem decently balanced so far ~Board game-esque exploration is visually pleasing and entertaining ~Mechanics are solid and easy to learn ~10 hours in and still finding new combos, and have only played 1/3 of the initial roster ~Interesting legacy system with currency to boost a struggling run (not microtransaction, earned in-game) CONS ~Poorly translated at times (easily patched but worth noting) ~Similar to StS, the game feels like its over right when i'm getting a good deck going. Needs longer modes. ~Some mechanics are confusing until tried. For example, keywords like "Transform" discards the card and makes a token during combat, but changes a card into something else permanently out of combat. ~Typos on certain things like "sepll" instead of "spell" (again, easily patched but worth noting) ~Asks for online server choice even though the game is entirely offline, so you must have internet to play. (Why?) All in all, with some polishing this game could be one of my go-to's. As it stands I will keep playing it for probably another 20 hours or so, unless something really keeps my attention. ~~Current Rating~~ 8/10

input_text: It's hard, it's a little sparse, and it's maybe not supported any more, but Deep In The Forest isn't bad. Graphically, it looks very polished. The art is lovely and has its own strong sense of style. But the game is made by a tiny team, so don't expect something as expansive as Slay The Spire. Instead, Deep is a relatively small-deck, combo-focused deckbuilding game. Mana accumulates rapidly, and you can mulch a card each turn to increase your mana gain, so the restriction on most of your turns is hand size. Beyond that, Slay The Spire is a pretty close comparison. You try to dps your enemies down before your turn ends and they damage you, and you have an inventory into which you can load passives to help you in fights. Unlike Slay, Deep has hard progression. Your deck and your level carry over from run to run, and I suspect you may need to grind them both to get past the first boss. This also means you can maybe accidentally build a garbage deck and have to reset your campaign, as combo synergy is *really* important in deep. Deep has an open map, and allows backtracks, but it tries to dissuade players from leveling up too much by causing all enemy damage values to go up the longer you take. This...doesn't interact perfectly with the leveling up system, but I guess it makes hard mode more exciting. I'll update this review if gameplay changes significantly as I continue, but as-is it's kind of a good time-kill. I don't feel the "just one more run" effect I get from Spire, and that's kind of a good thing. I can grind a bit, lose, and go back to what I was working on before I decided to take a break, rather than dumping a whole afternoon into a game. Edit: You have to grind for like an hour out of the gate, but after that the game gets pretty flexible and fun. There's room to explore a few different strategies, and later enemies have fairly complex behaviors (do X after you play two cards, do Y after you attack twice, do Z after you heal,) but you'll need to unlock some cards and gain a few levels to get to the good bits. If you get this, push past the three hour mark. It's much more rewarding than I expected. 2nd Edit: There are some weaknesses in the writing. Typos and strange grammar in a few places. They don't interfere with understanding the game mechanically (for the most part,) but the dialog after each boss is supposed to feel significant and dramatic, and the writing sometimes spoils that effect.

input_text: Fading Hearts is not one of those games which will really win an award for spelling, nor will its story win an Oscar by any means. Fading Hearts as a VN game is confident, but that comes with some spelling errors. So if you’re a grammar N…Z or an English teacher, it’s not advisable to pickup and play this game. It could possibly drive you insane by the spelling mistakes in this game. Also if by chance you’re picky on fictional settings and places not fitting in the logic of the real world then don’t pick this game up. But if you’re old enough to remember the ridiculous plots and plot holes of older Japanese VN games from the 80’s. Then you might have an idea what to expect as a back story plays out. In Fading Hearts Y2K led to a disaster which only affected one small nation in the whole world. That small nation is where our main catalog of characters in this game live. This leaves our main protagonist and his friends without parents because of the disaster which had befallen the small country of Sorayama. Personally, I had to stop playing for a bit because I was laughing for a while after reading it. But after getting my composure back I found out that I enjoyed Fading Hearts as a whole game. With all that said, technically the game does everything VN games have done in the past and doesn’t really break that mold. That is not really a bad thing as VN games were always about how you discovered the world around you, but also the people you interacted with. That in itself, is what Fading Hearts does right, it gives you the ability to choose how you want to pursue your relationship with those characters’. As well as how your choices will affect the final ending of the game itself. So if you’re a relaxed person whom happens not to get too stuck up on a few spelling errors and an off the wall notion of the world Ryou lives in, give this game at least a shot.

input_text: After several hours in this game, I have come mainly to one conclusion. I feel bad for the money I spent. The game is basically a mediocre shooter with mobile style controls (you autoaim nonstop with almost no control over where to aim) and there is a horrible grind to it. The graphics are servicable, the sound is servicable, nothing breathtaking. It's not technically *bad*. It just makes you wonder after paying 15 bucks what you paid for. The writing in the game contains errors after you switch to english, typos or even words leftover in french. There are no mouse controls but the game has buttons...? Why? Furthermore, the biggest challenge in the game is either being overwhelmed by enemies because you didn't grind enough to get better weapons, of which there are only 3 main weapons locked to shiptypes, minus the skills you use, OR the fact that some enemies can simply outright murder you without you having any chance to fight back. Some basic enemies can oneshot you with insanely fast missiles and they don't fire a single one, no, they fire several. Also they can and will fire from offscreen and they fly faster than anything else in this game, making dodging impossible. So you die randomly. Then you grind so you don't die. And even after that you still die. <- this is the non fun part The grind consists of running the same missions over and over again on easy mode, because there is literally no point in going for medium or hard since you get the same payout. And then you make like... in the beginning about 300 stars maybe? Middle game 700? depends where you grind and how good you are. And then you have upgrades that give you tiny advantages that cost you like 3000+ stars. Grind. Die. Repeat. Eventually you progress, which is not something you can really enjoy because all the game does is throw more enemies at you. I rarely had a moment where I can say "I got here because of skill, not luck". This is what pains me. The bossfights are decent, those are actually fun. They are not random. The bosses don't use unreasonable weapons to artificially make the game hard. The rest of the game is just a slog. For 12,49€... yeah, I should have gotten something better. The quality is not there and the game is ultimately not motivating.

input_text: The Translation's Power Level is Too Low Story If you judge the game based on the title, you're probably assuming that this is going to be similar to Final Fantasy IV. In reality, this game is an over-the-top Shonen anime power fantasy. While there is some overlap between JRPGs and the Shonen anime genre, this game has more Shonen tropes than the average JRPG. The protagonists are constantly in search of powerups to overcome the current unbeatable foe, only to overwhelm the boss once they get those powerups, and this repeats until the protagonists and enemies are god-tier. Many of the important duels and boss battles end with the main character getting knocked to low HP, only to get a scripted finishing move while spewing hammy lines, which I find oddly satisfying. If you enjoy Shonen anime, this is the game for you. If not, then I don't know what to say. For the most part, the plot is nothing too groundbreaking. You control a knight-turned-paladin who has to go around the world in order to stop a conspiracy of Extra Gems and Miasma. That said, the main characters are charming in their own ways, making the story enjoyable despite the clicheness. As for the villains, I enjoyed Red Rose, the second duel opponent, and the final chapter villain for their morally gray aspects. However, I think some major villains, such as Berienstahl and the Chapter 3 main antagonist, need more depth. That said, the plot point where we lose the first healer and the party gets framed is really contrived, since there's no effort to show fabricated evidence and therefore the healer should have no reason to believe in the party's guilt. Unfortunately, the current translation is terrible and pretty much reads like a barely edited machine translation, to the point where there are even untranslated lines. Worse yet, not everything is translated consistently, such as how the Flotsam is also called the Soaring Stone and how the dictionary uses both "Alec" and "Alex" as the name of the rival character. While the translation can be unintentionally funny at times, it can be very annoying for parts of the game where you have to make choices based on dialogue. It's a real shame, since I feel like the game would be a great Shonen power fantasy otherwise. Gameplay Yes, the Shonen tropes carry over into gameplay. The equipment system is set up so that the player can only change ornaments and skill gems while everything else is determined by the story. This allows the story to maintain relative power levels between the characters, since stats from equipment matter more than stats from leveling. Fortunately, the skill gem system is designed so that it's possible to make even low-tier characters effective as support casters for stronger characters, so it's still balanced in a way. Speaking of relative power balance, the Paladin class is designed to be overpowered, since it has very high stats and constantly learns new skills, making it a Super Swiss Army Knife. Normally, it's not good for one single character to carry all of the game's buff skills, but this is balanced by a mechanic that allows Nade to share his Paladin skills with other characters. This will make it easier to apply the Paladin's powerful buffs quicker, since the Paladin's skillset can be divided among five party members. One of my favorite features is the formation system, since it allows the player to cast an instant buff on the party and control how much enemy aggro the party members get. It reminds me of both the formation system from Nocturne: Rebirth and the Brave Order system of Trails of Cold Steel III/IV . That said, the game does throw a lot of miasma using enemies at the player in the endgame, meaning the Sword of Paladin formation ends up the only viable option for long battles. This is balanced by the Commander gem, which gives access to other formations' buffs. The game has a duel system that works similarly to Suikoden . Melee allows Nade to guard against a ranged attack before striking back, ranged attacks can safely damage a countering enemy, and counterattack allows Nade to negate a melee attack before striking back. This requires the player to memorize the enemy's dialogue to figure out which action they're going to do, though later battles also require the player to memorize facial expressions. Sadly, this system has two major pitfalls. One is that melee vs ranged still results in damage to the melee user, which is bad for the player on hard mode because they'll still take more damage to their total percentage of health than the enemy. The other flaw is that the bad translation can make it hard to discern the enemy's intention. As for the game's difficulty, I played most of the game on hard mode. It's fairly balanced, but the difficulty can fluctuate a lot due to the story-enforced power levels. Once Nade gets his Paladin abilities, he's very powerful compared to even bosses and shouldn't have much trouble at all. However, when the game forces the player to control a party of lower-tier characters, the difficulty skyrockets, though it's still possible to win all the mandatory battles with some effort. Verdict 7/10, this game is the embodiment of the meme, "I have the power of God and anime on my side!" The game has a decent story and is well-balanced for the most part. However, the translation doesn't do the game justice at all. I really hope the game will get a better retranslation in the future so that it'll be easier to appreciate its sheer Shonen anime energy.

input_text: This game is tons of fun. I don’t remember the last time a game made me laugh so much. I bought it because I wanted a classic turn-based RPG game with nice art and good story. It has all that and more. So, here are the good points. The art is great. The Celestials are the best-looking characters ever. The story is great and shines even through the bad translation. Lots of humor. The MC and other human warriors are the “brawn no brain” type and that leads to hilarious dialogues. Celestials are on a different level, they crack jokes intentionally. I loved Ishbel’s insolent sarcasm and Siegfried’s morbid jokes. Unfortunately, we only get about 40% of it, the rest is lost in the translation and the only way you could guess there was a joke is because the dialogue looks particularly awkward. Still, enough come through to make you laugh. Characters. Again, they are on two different levels. Humans are very cliché, nothing to say about them. Celestials are intriguing, they have complex past stories and relationships that the main story only hints on. Wish I could know more. Autobattler! It’s epic. It starts as a standard plot with the kids as main characters, but before you even get to the mid-game, you start recruiting the godlike Tetrarchs into your party. Next thing you know, you play with demi-god characters with abilities on par with their high stats. Yeah, I know, it’s all balanced and the enemies can thwart their efforts, but I don’t care, I just love to see Siegfrid use that insta-kill spell. Not intentionally, translation bloopers make it hilarious. So do the outrageous stats. After they reached level 25, I found myself saying “my attack stat is WHAT now?” a lot. Really, when do you see your attack going over a thousand? It gets better, you have an achievement to do 3,000 in one blow. Once you do that, there is 10,000. Then 30,000. And yes, you can do all that. I couldn’t help laughing when I did it, it’s just so unusual, yet, so appropriate for having demi-gods in your party. Well, there are cons. The translation is very uneven and seems to be done by at least two different people, if not more. The worst part is the skill descriptions. The person who translated it had no idea what increase and decrease mean. Do not trust the descriptions, just try the skill out and see what it really does. It’s simple enough to figure out. It’s easy to learn and easy to play. Some people may see it as not enough challenge. I love to tinker with the party composition and equipment, so I loved it, but that’s your primary challenge. If you are looking for something else, you may be disappointed. In conclusion, yes, do buy this.

input_text: Positives Plot: I thought the plot and premise was quite good. I don't know why but I kept thinking of a game called The Dig whilst playing this, got a similar vibe for some reason. I'll comment later on in the review how this was let down in some ways but otherwise it's one of the more interesting hidden object games on Steam. Aesthetics: Some locations look a bit too similar IMO but that doesn't stop the game looking pretty. The music was also quite atmospheric which is always nice in a HOG. The UI is okay but getting the inventory bar out of the way got a bit annoying sometimes ;) Achievements: While some might see this as a negative it was a nice break to play a HOG without any punishing achievements! Depending on the difficulty level you play through, you can also get them all in one run which may appeal to some people :) Value for money: I got just over 3 hours of play time out of this game and for once it wasn't one I'd leave running in the background while I wandered off to do something else. That was one full run through then a short play through just to get one of the achievements I'd missed, so to me this game has paid for itself in game time. There are games on Steam for more money than this that offer less content! Hints: I was getting butt mad and was going to review this game differently until I realised it was my own fault I was struggling! Use the little mobile PC in the bottom left of the screen, it contains a lot of information that will help you. I assumed it would just be like the typical HOG diary and log what you had done but it actually gives you some nice little hints ;) Puzzles: The puzzles in this game are a lot easier than other HOGs on Steam IMO but I didn't see this as a bad thing, the game more than makes up for it with the hidden object puzzles, of which there are a-plenty ;) Negatives Backpedalling: Maybe it's just me but I get bored quite quickly with hidden object games that require a lot of clicking back and forth between screens to trigger events. There isn't too much of it in this game, but there are times where you will be looking around for ages trying to figure out where to go and it's because the screen you were on ten minutes ago has an event but because you didn't go back to it immediately after leaving that screen. Cut scenes: Don't hate me but I can be super impatient, so waiting for an oiler to oil four seperate pieces of machinery really slowly just sets me off haha! I wish some of the actions and cut scenes were a bit faster, purely because I want to get back to the game. Just personal preference though ;D Text: The only thing I really disliked with any depth was the text in this game. I think the vibe the developers were going for was great, but it was ruined by multiple typos and poor translations. This isn't the only HOG on Steam to have this problem, and it doesn't make me think any less of the game but I think it's selling the game and all the hard work put into it short. TLDR: A nice take plot wise, two seperate teams were an interesting concept. Marred by some poor translations/typos and occasional backpedal frenzies but otherwise a well thought out HOG that is definitely every bit a HOG! Lots of hidden object puzzles that are challenging at times. If you're looking for a relaxed game that is easy to 100% then Mystery of a Lost Planet is a bargain :)

input_text: The translation is bad, at some points entirely unintelligible. The game play is decent at best, fairly mediocre for a tactics game. The adult content is mediocre at best. The game falsely advertises: 200 different weapons You can craft 5 or so variants of about 10 categories of weapons (with each variant having about 5 upgrades) = 50 "types of weapons" with 5 upgrades each = 250 items There is a couple of unique items you can get though. But I would hardly call this game having 200 actually different weapons. The real reason you should NOT buy this game is that it has an Game-ENDING glitch in Mission 11 (that has been known by the developer since 2019 and still no fix). So in Mission 11 you get a mission that starts out pretty much like the previous 10 missions: Cutscene -> Enemy Placement -> Game Play (Kill all enemy units). In this mission you however get a fairly large number of friendly units and a fairly large amount of enemies. No problem. EXCEPT the fact that one of your friendly units is PLACED ontop of an enemy unit, which glitches this unit out so that the game thinks it is friendly during your and friendly unit's turn, but the glitched enemy can attack you and the friendly units during its turn. So an enemy you can not kill in a battle where you have to kill all enemies. That is GAME-ENDING. And not only can you not kill this glitched enemy, if it attacks one of your friendly units the game will crash, so both Game-ENDING and Game-Crashing. So if this issue was fixed I might consider re-reviewing the game. If you consider this game for its Tactics game-play get Wargroove instead. If you consider this game for its adult content get another game with better quality art and better game play.

input_text: Great RM title that suffers from some grammar issues but has a solid core and decent story. Includes a free soundtrack, too! Aside from some minor translation errors (improper use of words and spelling mistakes) that are common with most RPG Maker games, this is actually a solid, well-built title. The amount of scripts used in the game (IYKYK) seems daunting, as the more you add to an RM game the more it tends to mess things up, but things gel and work cohesively very well. I've encountered only mild slow-down issues (the game suddenly drops to 5-10FPS) with the Dev having stated they are working on fixing it. A crude workaround is to hit Alt+Enter to make it switch between windowed and fullscreen or vice-versa As for the story, it's actually intriguing. The aforementioned typos are a little off-putting, but it is well crafted and has kept my attention so far. The puzzles are standard, with only one giving me serious pause until I figured out the trick. Then, it was actually rather ingenious in how simply it actually was. Is it worth the price? I got it on sale for around 5 bucks CAD, but I would say it's well worth the full price, and a must-buy on sale if you're a fan of games of this type. For an RM game it has a surprising amount of polish. Also of note: the launcher they included with the game and the extras. I LOVE THEM. It's something I think ALL RM games could benefit from, as it lets you decide if you want to start the game in fullscreen or windowed, and what ratio to make the game screen. It also offers direct links to where they are on your drive (no digging around) to the artbook AND it comes with a full soundtrack which was not mentioned on the Store Page. Bonus!

input_text: My Goddess's Deck Has No Pathetic Cards Story There isn't much of a story here. Basically, your protagonist, Fatima, is the guardian priestess of a nation, Donerksela, and she must help them manage their resources in order to expand their population and increase her power. Sadly, we don't really get much more dialogue than that. Some of the choices can let you be more lenient when it comes to your citizens' workload, but that's about it. We also never learn what's up with the enemies that show up, but the last guardian apparently failed to defeat them. All we know is that once the final boss is defeated on week 90, your protagonist is able to become a goddess or maybe something worse depending on your alignment. Your alignment stat determines what your character will look like, but I have no idea if going for negative alignment significantly changes the story. It probably doesn't change much, since there's no cutscene for winning the game. Personally, I'd like to see how ascending to goddesshood affects Fatima's relationship with her citizens. Gameplay As implied by the above section, the game is all about the resource management and card gameplay. You get a randomized board to build facilities on, and each tile has a preset type of facility you are allowed to build, but some cards allow you to override that restriction. Each facility also has durability that you have to look out for, though at high levels, you might not have to worry about that durability outside of friendly fire with your offensive cards. You generate a certain amount of resources each week depending on your facilities, so try to strike a balance so that you have every resource you need. However, to ensure you can't do a ton of stuff in one week, you have a set amount of EP that gets refilled each week. But what exactly are you spending resources on? Food is spent to increase your population, wood is spent to increase your population cap, gold is spent on passives in the study menu, fuel is spent on repairs and manipulating your hand of cards, and ore is spent on facility upgrades. Passive skills in the study require almost all types of resources, and the nodes you can upgrade are randomized, though you can spend more resources to change a node to something else. Enemies can inflict debuffs on you to slow down your resource production and they will also take up tiles on the map. Worse yet, they can attack your population, causing a game over if your population is wiped out. Because of this, you may want to store up some offensive cards while lowering the enemy spawn rate in the study menu. However, you still need some enemies to show up if you want to farm money for the shop. As for the bosses, which appear every 30 weeks, they have a lot of HP, clear all your resources, and deal massive population damage, but if you win, you get to pick a powerful relic to add a strong passive for the rest of the run. You can gain EXP and manipulate your alignment score to evolve Fatima into her next form. I'm not sure how this affects gameplay outside of aesthetics though. I think some transformations increase the number of card slots, which can help with stockpiling offensive cards. Evolution also unlocks the game animation speed setting in the options menu, but it feels wrong to hide such a feature behind game progress. Verdict 7/10 Once you get a hang of the mechanics, a casual run is fairly well-balanced, though the beginning of the game will be the hardest due to your lack of EP and card slots. Towards the end, you should have so many resources and passive buffs that you actually will feel like a goddess. Unfortunately, the game doesn't have much of a story and the translation is terrible, which makes it harder to learn from the tutorials and in-game manual. Maybe this would be better as a phone game considering how the gameplay loop works.
